books.title: Life at the Pond
books.art_why: Pond animals, plants and their watery habitat exist today and are ideal for real photographs.

pages.text: The pond shines in the sun. The water is quiet. Many things live in the pond. It is home to many reptiles and other animals. It is home to many plants and fish. The pond is like a small world.
pages.brief: A wide, sunlit pond with calm, quiet water. Green plants grow at the edges and beneath the surface. A turtle rests at the bank, a reptile sharing the pond with other animals. Small fish swim in the clear water. The pond stretches out like a small world.

pages.text: Around the pond, ducks feed and play. They gobble tiny plants and dive to catch small fish. Mama duck watches her babies learn to swim. What fun! How yummy! The big blue heron spears a fish and gobbles it whole. Some of them snap up flying insects. Big and small birds feed by the pond.
pages.brief: Around the pond, ducks feed and play. Ducklings paddle while mama duck watches them learn to swim. One duck gobbles tiny plants, another dives for small fish. A tall blue heron spears a fish and swallows it whole. Small birds snap up flying insects; big and small birds feed by the water.

pages.text: The top of the water is like a thin sheet. Insects skate, hop, and float on it. The water strider skates on long legs. The springtail hops across with its tail. Here we go! The roots and stems are under the water, way at the bottom. Lily pads with pretty flowers float on top. They have eyes on each side, to look up and down. Whirligig beetles spin on the water.
pages.brief: On the pond's surface, insects skate, hop and float. A water strider glides on long legs; a springtail hops with its tail. Whirligig beetles spin, eyes on each side to look up and down. Below, roots and stems reach down to the bottom. Lily pads with pretty flowers float on top.

pages.text: Frogs begin as tiny eggs in the water. The eggs become wiggly tadpoles, and the tadpoles grow into frogs with legs. They jump in and out of the water looking for food. Chug-a-rumm! He has a very loud croak that sounds like Chug-a-rumm. He makes a big splash when he jumps in. The bullfrog is one of the biggest frogs.
pages.brief: Tiny frog eggs in the water become wiggly tadpoles. The tadpoles grow legs and turn into frogs that jump in and out of the water looking for food. A big bullfrog, one of the biggest frogs, croaks loudly and makes a big splash as it jumps in.

pages.text: What is that pile of sticks in the water? Beavers have built a house for their family. When a beaver swims, it smacks the water with its tail. Smack! on a big log in the water. When it gets warm, they sun themselves In winter, the turtles sleep down in the mud. Turtles in the pond snap up little fish to eat.
pages.brief: A pile of sticks sits in the water, a beaver's house built for its family. A beaver swims and smacks the water with its tail on a big log. Turtles sun themselves when it gets warm; in winter they sleep down in the mud. Turtles snap up little fish to eat.

pages.text: Fish of many sizes and colors swim in the pond. They breathe under the water. Down in the mud, mama fish lays eggs. Later on, papa fish watches the babies. What a fun world! bugs and turtles, and many plants all live together. The pond is a small world where birds and fish.
pages.brief: Fish of many sizes and colors swim through the pond, breathing under the water. Down in the mud, a mama fish lays eggs; later a papa fish watches the babies. Bugs, turtles and many plants live together here. The pond is a small world where birds and fish share the water.

books.title: Discovering Dinosaurs
books.art_why: Dinosaurs and fossil digs are prehistoric, so real photographs of these animals and events are impossible.

pages.text: Finding Fossils How do we know dinosaurs lived on Earth? We know because we have found fossils in rocks all over the world.
pages.brief: Rocks holding fossil shapes lie in many different places around the world, from rocky hills to open ground, showing that fossils have been found across the Earth.

pages.text: Scientists have found fossils of dinosaur bones, footprints, teeth, nests, and eggs.
pages.brief: A spread of dinosaur fossils rests together: large bones, a three-toed footprint, sharp teeth, a nest, and eggs, all found preserved in rock by scientists.

pages.text: These scientists are carefully digging dinosaur fossils out of the ground. They will wrap up the fossils to keep them safe. Then they will take them to a.
pages.brief: Scientists kneel at a dig site, carefully digging dinosaur fossils out of the ground with small tools. Nearby, wrapped fossils are being made safe for the journey to a museum.

pages.text: At the museum, scientists will study the fossils. They try to fit bone fossils together Some pieces of the skeleton might be missing. Scientists use what they know about other animals to make pieces fit.
pages.brief: Inside a museum, scientists study fossil bones on a work table. They fit bone pieces together into a skeleton, using what they know about other animals to help fill the missing parts.

pages.text: Learning from Fossils Scientists study other animals to learn about dinosaurs. Dinosaur bones may be bigger. But many are shaped the same.
pages.brief: A scientist looks closely at the bones of a modern animal beside a large dinosaur bone. The dinosaur bone is bigger, but many bones are shaped the same.

pages.text: Scientists compare dinosaur bone fossils to other animals. They learn that some dinosaurs walked, and some flew.
pages.brief: Scientists compare dinosaur bone fossils with bones from other animals. Beside them, one dinosaur is shown walking on land while another is shown flying.

pages.text: Scientists study fossil footprints to see how fast dinosaurs moved. Some dinosaurs moved very slowly. Some moved faster than humans.
pages.brief: Scientists study fossil dinosaur footprints in the ground. The footprints show that some dinosaurs moved very slowly, while others moved faster than humans.

pages.text: Scientists study fossil teeth to learn what dinosaurs ate. Some teeth are sharp like the teeth of meat eaters. Other teeth are flat like the teeth of plant eaters.
pages.brief: Scientists examine fossil dinosaur teeth. Some teeth are sharp, like the teeth of meat eaters, while other teeth are flat, like the teeth of plant eaters.

pages.text: Scientists learn about dinosaur babies from fossil nests and eggs. Some dinosaurs may have sat on their eggs like many birds do.
pages.brief: Scientists look at a fossil dinosaur nest with eggs inside. Nearby, a dinosaur is shown sitting on its eggs, the way many birds do.

pages.text: Scientists also find fossils of plants, fish, insects, and other animals. These fossils help them learn what Earth was like when dinosaurs lived here.
pages.brief: Fossils of plants, fish, insects, and other animals lie in the rock around dinosaur fossils, helping scientists learn what Earth was like when dinosaurs lived.

pages.text: How Long Ago? Scientists study rocks where fossils are found. Older fossils are deeper in the ground than newer fossils.
pages.brief: Scientists study layers of rock where fossils are found. Fossils deeper down in the ground are older, while fossils closer to the surface are newer.

pages.text: No one knows for sure why the dinosaurs disappeared millions of years ago.
pages.brief: A group of dinosaurs stands in a prehistoric landscape, millions of years ago. No one knows for sure why the dinosaurs disappeared.

books.title: Birds
books.art_why: All birds shown are real animals that can be photographed.

pages.text: This pelican has a big, long beak. There is a deep sac of skin under its beak. The sac holds fish that the pelican scoops up from the water. The roadrunner runs very fast to get its food. It eats fast lizards, snakes, and bugs. It lives in the desert and spends most of its time on the ground. This bird is a roadrunner.
pages.brief: A pelican stands near water with a big, long beak and a deep sac of skin underneath, holding fish it has scooped up. Nearby, a roadrunner runs fast on the desert ground, chasing fast lizards, snakes, and bugs for food.

pages.text: This toucan lives in the rainforest. It has a big, colorful beak. It uses its beak to pick fruit from trees. It can run very fast to get away from danger. But it has very long, strong legs. It cannot fly because it has small wings for such a large body. This big bird is an emu.
pages.brief: A toucan in the rainforest has a big, colorful beak and uses it to pick fruit from a tree. An emu stands on the ground on long, strong legs, with small wings for its large body, running fast to get away from danger.

pages.text: This puffin eats small fish. It is short and fat and has a colorful beak. Puffins look funny on land. But they spend most of their time in the sea. pages.brief: A short, fat puffin with a colorful beak eats small fish, looks funny on land, and swims underwater using its wings. An owl with big eyes and very soft feathers comes out at night, able to see in the dark and fly without making a sound.

pages.text: Hummingbirds are the smallest birds. They are bright and colorful. They can stay in one place when they fly. pages.brief: Tiny, bright, colorful hummingbirds hover in one place as they fly, using long beaks and tongues to get food from flowers. High above land and water, eagles with sharp claws and beaks spot snakes, mice, and fish, then use their feet and beaks to catch food and rip it apart.

pages.text: Cockatoos have thick, sharp beaks that can crack open hard nuts. Cockatoos live in large groups. They can be very loud. The holes help them to smell food from far away. Many have big holes in their beaks. Many have no feathers on their heads. Vultures eat dead animals.
pages.brief: Cockatoos with thick, sharp beaks crack open hard nuts and gather in large, loud groups. Vultures eat dead animals; many have no feathers on their heads and big holes in their beaks that help them smell food from far away.

books.title: Is That a Fish?
books.art_why: Fish, sharks, seahorses and rays are real animals that can be photographed.

pages.text: What Are Fish? What does a fish look like? You might be surprised.
pages.brief: A fish is shown on its own, with an appearance that invites a surprised reaction. The picture leaves open what a fish looks like, since a fish may not look the way someone expects when they first see one.

pages.text: Fish can be very big or very small. This shark is the largest fish in the world. Like other fish, it has a backbone. It breathes through gills. It has fins to help it swim.
pages.brief: A very large shark, the largest fish in the world, swims through the water. Its backbone, gills and fins are visible as it moves, showing how this fish breathes through gills and uses fins to swim.

pages.text: Some fish look like other animals. This fish is called a seahorse. The fin on the back of the seahorse beats very fast. This is how the seahorse moves around.
pages.brief: A seahorse is shown as a fish that looks like another animal. Its body is visible as the fin on its back beats very fast, and this rapid movement is what lets the seahorse move around.

pages.text: A seahorse uses its tail to grab onto plants in the water. It can hide in the plants where no hungry fish can find it.
pages.brief: A seahorse uses its tail to grab onto plants in the water. It hides among the plants, where no hungry fish can find it, keeping the small seahorse hidden safely among the nearby water plants.

pages.text: This fish, called an eel, looks It swims by moving its whole body. It can swim forward and backward. It breathes by opening and closing its mouth to pump water over its gills.
pages.brief: An eel is shown as a fish in the water. It swims by moving its whole body, forward and backward, and it breathes by opening and closing its mouth to pump water over its gills.

pages.text: Rays This large, flat fish is called a ray. It has wing-like fins that help it glide through the water.
pages.brief: A large, flat fish called a ray is shown in the water. Its wing-like fins spread out on either side as it glides through the water, showing the shape and movement of this flat fish.

pages.text: Some rays have spines on their tails. They use the spines to sting their prey. Rays can hide on the bottom of the sea.
pages.brief: A ray is shown with spines on its tail. It uses these spines to sting its prey, and it can hide on the bottom of the sea, where its flat body rests out of sight.

pages.text: Fish Out of Water This fish lives on mud flats. When the tide goes out, the fish can stay on the land until the water comes back. It breathes through its skin.
pages.brief: A fish is shown out of water on a mud flat after the tide has gone out. It stays on the land until the water comes back, breathing through its skin while it waits on the mud.

pages.text: This fish sometimes comes onto the land to look for fresh water. It wiggles its tail and props its body up on its fins when it moves. This makes it look like the fish can walk.
pages.brief: A fish is shown on land, coming onto the land to look for fresh water. It wiggles its tail and props its body up on its fins as it moves, making it look as if the fish can walk.

pages.text: Is That a Fish? Fish can be many colors, sizes, and shapes. They can move in different ways.
pages.brief: Several fish are shown together in the water in many different colors, sizes and shapes. Each one moves in a different way, showing how varied fish can be in color, size, shape and movement.

pages.text: What will you see the next time you close your eyes and picture a fish?
pages.brief: A fish is shown as a picture in the mind, after eyes close. The scene leaves open what kind of fish will be pictured, asking what will be seen the next time eyes close and a fish comes to mind.

books.title: Hibernation
books.art_why: Real hibernating animals and habitats can be photographed today.

pages.text: No Food in Winter Many places have cold winters. Some animals in these places have trouble finding food in the winter. Many animals move to warmer places to find food. Other animals hibernate.
pages.brief: A wide, snowy winter landscape with bare trees and frozen ground. In the foreground a few small animals trek away across the snow toward a distant, brighter hillside, while nearby another animal lies curled up tightly asleep in a sheltered spot under roots, still and quiet in the cold.

pages.text: What Is Hibernating? Hibernating is like a very sound sleep. Hibernating animals sleep for many days or weeks at a time. Animals breathe slowly when they hibernate. Their hearts beat slower, and they do not need to eat.
pages.brief: Close view of a hibernating animal curled into a snug ball inside a nest of dry leaves and grass. Its eyes are closed, its body still, its breathing slow and shallow. The scene is calm and dim, showing the animal deep in a long, sound sleep, undisturbed and peaceful.

pages.text: How Do They Stay Alive? Hibernating animals eat lots of food before winter begins. They store the food in their bodies as fat. Their bodies live off this fat while they sleep.
pages.brief: An animal in late autumn eats eagerly beside a bush heavy with berries and scattered nuts, its cheeks full and its body round and plump. Fallen leaves lie on the ground around it. The animal is feeding heavily, building up fat in its body before the cold winter arrives.

pages.text: They also need a safe place to sleep. They need to be safe from the cold. And they need to be safe from predators that want to eat them.
pages.brief: A cutaway view of a safe den beneath tree roots, where a small animal sleeps tucked in dry leaves, sheltered from the cold outside. Beyond the entrance, in the snow, a predator prowls past, sniffing. The sleeping animal is hidden and protected, deep inside its secure, sheltered sleeping place.

pages.text: Some animals, like bats, hibernate in caves. Hibernating snakes sleep underground in burrows. Frogs and turtles sleep in mud at the bottom of ponds.
pages.brief: Three habitats shown together: a dark cave ceiling with bats hanging asleep; a cutaway of an underground burrow where snakes lie coiled in the soil; and the muddy bottom of a pond where frogs and turtles rest half-buried in the thick mud beneath the water.

pages.text: Hibernating Animals Groundhogs, chipmunks, and snakes hibernate. Frogs, turtles, and prairie dogs hibernate. Hamsters and hedgehogs hibernate. Even bees and snails hibernate!
pages.brief: A busy nature scene gathering many hibernating animals: a groundhog, a chipmunk, snakes, frogs, turtles, prairie dogs, a hamster, a hedgehog, bees and snails, each shown in its own small patch of grass, soil, water or burrow, all settled and resting in their places.

pages.text: Some mice, squirrels, and bats hibernate all winter long. Bears, badgers, and skunks might wake up to eat on a warm day. Then they go back to sleep. In the spring, all the hibernating animals wake up.
pages.brief: A winter scene with mice, squirrels and bats asleep in holes, nests and a cave, sleeping through the cold months. On a mild, sunny day a bear, badger and skunk stir and wake briefly near their dens; then spring arrives with green shoots, and all the hibernating animals wake and emerge.

books.title: Fantastic Flying Machines
books.art_why: Flying machines and flight history can be shown with real photographs.

pages.text: People always wanted to fly. Some made wings out of wood. One artist drew a plan for a helicopter hundreds of years ago! Other people built strange gliders. Two brothers made the first hot-air balloon. History of Flight.
pages.brief: People throughout history try to fly: one person wears wings made of wood, an artist sketches a helicopter plan, others stand by strange gliders, and two brothers stand beside the first hot-air balloon. The scene shows early attempts at flight.

pages.text: Wilbur Wright watches his brother Orville make his famous flight. Airplanes use engines to stay in the air. The Wright brothers built the first airplane that worked. People could fly! Now, large planes can carry your family on vacation. Airplanes have changed a lot since the early days of flight. Airplanes.
pages.brief: Wilbur Wright stands on the ground watching his brother Orville make his famous flight in the first working airplane. A modern large airplane carries a family on vacation. The scene shows early flight and a later airplane with engines.

pages.text: Some planes today use strong jet engines. They help planes fly high and fast. engines. Propeller blades spin like a fan’s blades. Planes that fly low or slow often use propeller.
pages.brief: A plane with strong jet engines flies high and fast in the sky. Another plane with propeller blades, spinning like a fan, flies low and slow. The jet engine and the propeller are shown clearly on the aircraft.

pages.text: Planes carry things quickly over long distances. Planes carry cargo all around the world. almost anywhere. direction. They can take off straight up and can land Helicopters fly differently from planes. They can fly in any Helicopters.
pages.brief: A cargo plane carries boxes quickly over a long distance around the world. A helicopter takes off straight up and lands in any direction, flying differently from planes. Both flying machines are shown in the sky above the ground.

pages.text: Flying in a helicopter saves time. Helicopters are used to quickly help people who are lost or hurt. Unlike other flying machines, you can’t steer them. Hot-air balloons are quiet. They are pushed by the wind. Blimps and Balloons.
pages.brief: A helicopter flies quickly to help people who are lost or hurt. Nearby, a quiet hot-air balloon is pushed by the wind, with no steering. The helicopter and the balloon are shown in the sky, with people on the ground waiting for help.

pages.text: Blimps are like long balloons. Blimps have engines and are steered by pilots. Have you seen a blimp? Where would you like to fly? Airplanes fly everywhere. for a ride. A hot-air balloon can take you A hang glider drifts on a breeze. There are many ways to fly. Other Ways to Fly.
pages.brief: A long blimp with engines is steered by a pilot in the sky. A hot-air balloon takes a person for a ride, and a hang glider drifts on a breeze. Airplanes fly everywhere above them, showing many ways to fly.

books.title: Jane Goodall
books.art_why: Jane Goodall is a real person, and photographs of her, the chimpanzees and the Gombe forest exist.

pages.text: The Watcher As a young girl, Jane Goodall loved to watch animals. She read about them, too. She dreamed of living in Africa one day. She hoped to write about the wild animals there.
pages.brief: A young girl named Jane Goodall sits by a window, watching birds and small animals outside. A stack of animal books rests beside her. She looks thoughtful, gazing into the distance as if dreaming of faraway Africa.

pages.text: Off to Africa When she was old enough, Goodall worked and saved her money. When she had saved enough, she went on a trip to Africa. In Africa, Goodall met a famous.
pages.brief: Young Jane Goodall steps off a boat onto a sunny African dock, holding a travel bag. She shakes hands with a famous scientist who has come to meet her. Water and a boat are visible behind her.

pages.text: The scientist needed help with a new study about chimpanzees. The study would look at how they behave. He asked Goodall to work on the study with him.
pages.brief: The famous scientist sits at a table with young Jane Goodall, leaning forward as he explains a new study about chimpanzees and how they behave. He gestures with one hand, asking her to join the work.

pages.text: Into the Forest To work on the study, Goodall moved to the Gombe (GOME-bay) She watched the chimps every day.
pages.brief: Jane Goodall sits quietly in the green Gombe forest, watching a group of chimpanzees move through the trees. Dappled sunlight falls through the leaves. She is still and patient, observing the chimps every day from a respectful distance.

pages.text: The Gombe Gang At first, most of the chimps were afraid of Goodall. Only a chimp she named David trusted her. He let Goodall meet his family.
pages.brief: Most chimpanzees keep their distance, watching Jane Goodall from the trees. Only a chimp named David comes close, calm and curious. He leads her to meet his family, a group of chimpanzees gathered nearby in the forest.

pages.text: Goodall took notes about the Her notes upset many scientists. They had their own ideas about how chimps behaved.
pages.brief: Jane Goodall kneels in the forest, writing notes in a notebook about the chimpanzees as they play nearby. In a separate office, scientists frown over papers, upset by her ideas and holding their own views.

pages.text: Goodall said chimps were smart. She said they used sticks as tools to dig up bugs to eat. She also said chimps showed feelings, as humans do.
pages.brief: A chimpanzee uses a thin stick to dig bugs out of a mound, while Jane Goodall watches closely. The chimp looks clever and focused. This shows how chimps use tools and seem to have feelings.

pages.text: Goodall saw chimps that were happy, sad, and angry. She saw that each chimp behaved in its own way, just as humans do.
pages.brief: Three chimpanzees show different feelings: one looks happy and playful, one sad and quiet, one angry with a scowl. Each chimp behaves in its own way, just as people do. They sit among the forest trees.

pages.text: Goodall’s work made some scientists think again about chimps. They saw that some of their old ideas might be wrong.
pages.brief: A group of scientists sit around a table in a quiet room, looking at notes and thinking carefully. Their faces show surprise and doubt as they reconsider their old ideas about chimpanzees after Jane Goodall's work.

pages.text: Trouble in the Forest After many years in Gombe, Goodall became worried. Many people in this part of Africa are very poor. Some were cutting down the forest for firewood or to grow crops there. Some were stealing baby chimps and selling them.
pages.brief: In the African forest, people cut down trees for firewood and clear land for crops. Tree stumps dot the ground, and the forest looks thin. Nearby, a baby chimpanzee sits in a small cage, taken to be sold.

pages.text: Goodall knew what she had to do. She went around the world, talking about her work. She asked for help to save the chimps and the forest. People trusted her. They helped to support her work.
pages.brief: Jane Goodall stands before a large audience, speaking about her work and asking for help to save the chimpanzees and the forest. People listen closely, trust her, and offer their support with warm, attentive faces.

pages.text: The Work Goes On Goodall died in October 2025. She is remembered for her work to protect the forest and the chimpanzees. People make sure her work continues. To learn more, go to: www.rootsandshoots.org and www.janegoodall.org.
pages.brief: An older Jane Goodall stands among chimpanzees and tall forest trees, smiling gently. Around her, people continue her work, caring for the forest and the chimpanzees she loved. Sunlight filters through the green leaves in a quiet, hopeful scene.

books.title: Bigger Than a Monster Truck
books.art_why: The book includes ancient and future vehicles alongside giant machines, so drawing suits it.

pages.text: Vehicles That Move Things and People Vehicles That Dig.
pages.brief: A huge passenger-and-supply vehicle moves along a road, carrying people and goods. Beside it, a heavy digging machine with a large bucket lowers into the ground, ready to scoop earth. The two machines show vehicles that move things and people and vehicles that dig.

pages.text: Big Movers Have you ever seen a monster truck? Monster trucks have big wheels and can drive over almost any obstacle in their path. As gigantic as monster trucks are, though, some vehicles are even bigger.
pages.brief: A monster truck with enormous wheels drives over a rugged obstacle, its big tires crushing the ground. Beyond it, a much larger vehicle looms, making the monster truck look small. The scene shows that some vehicles are even bigger than monster trucks.

pages.text: Vehicles That Move Things and People The Duck The “Duck” is a truck that can travel on both land and water. On land, the Duck travels on six wheels, but in water, the Duck uses a propeller. The Duck can carry passengers and supplies to locations that are hard to reach. Rescue workers sometimes use this truck to evacuate people caught in storms. You can even ride a Duck for fun in some places.
pages.brief: A six-wheeled Duck truck rolls on land toward a shoreline, carrying passengers and supplies. In the water, the same truck uses a propeller. Nearby, rescue workers help people caught in a storm, and riders enjoy a Duck ride for fun.

pages.text: Vehicle Bridge This amazing machine is both a vehicle and a bridge. The vehicle bridge is used in places where there are no roads or bridges. The vehicle moves the bridge into place. Then the bridge unfolds itself over the gap, allowing other vehicles to drive across. When the bridge is no longer needed, it folds up onto the vehicle.
pages.brief: A vehicle bridge sits at the edge of a gap where there are no roads or bridges. It moves its bridge into place, then unfolds the bridge over the gap. Other vehicles drive across, and later the bridge folds back onto the vehicle.

pages.text: Cranes Cranes lift and move heavy objects from one location to another. These machines help workers construct buildings and load and unload cargo. Some of the world’s largest cranes move containers from ships to land. Others are used to lift supplies to the tops of skyscrapers.
pages.brief: Large cranes lift heavy objects at a busy port, moving containers from a ship onto land. Other cranes help workers construct a building and lift supplies to the top of a skyscraper. The machines load and unload cargo and move heavy loads from place to place.

pages.text: Dump Trucks The world’s biggest dump trucks are found at mines. Miners use these trucks to haul loads of rocks and dirt. Some trucks can transport up to four hundred tons of soil per load. Because they carry such heavy loads, they use some of the biggest tires in the world. Their tires are over 13 feet (4 m) tall—twice as tall as a person.
pages.brief: At a mine, miners use a giant dump truck to haul a load of rocks and dirt. The truck’s tires are over thirteen feet tall, twice as tall as a person standing beside them. The truck can carry up to four hundred tons of soil in one load.

pages.text: Overland Trains These giant trains were built to haul loads to remote places without roads. The trains travel on huge wheels instead of on train tracks. Each wheel is about 10 feet (3 m) high and has its own motor. The longest overland train was almost 600 feet (183 m) long and pulled twelve cars. The lead car held six people, beds, and a kitchen.
pages.brief: A very long overland train with twelve cars rolls across remote land without roads, using huge wheels instead of train tracks. Each wheel has its own motor, and the lead car carries six people, beds, and a kitchen.

pages.text: Moving Space Vehicles Some of the world’s biggest vehicles were made to move spacecraft. These “crawler transporters” carry rockets, space shuttles, and other vehicles on a platform two stories high. These vehicles are so wide that they need their own road. Computers and a team of thirty people help these huge machines move.
pages.brief: A crawler transporter carries a rocket and a space shuttle on a platform two stories high along a wide road of its own. A team of thirty people and computers help the huge machine move the spacecraft slowly and carefully.

pages.text: Vehicles That Dig Giant Power Shovels Miners use giant power shovels to dig loads of rocks and dirt out of a mine. Power shovels have a big bucket that can break into the earth and scoop it up, and these complex machines can be as tall as a sixteen-story building.
pages.brief: At a mine, miners use a giant power shovel to dig rocks and dirt. The shovel’s big bucket breaks into the earth and scoops up a load. The complex machine stands as tall as a sixteen-story building.

pages.text: Tunnel Diggers Tunneling machines dig tunnels under the earth, even moving through solid rock. They use a drill to dig through the ground. These machines dug three tunnels under the ocean between England and France that are big enough for large trains to pass through.
pages.brief: A tunneling machine with a powerful drill digs underground, cutting through solid rock. Its tunnel is large enough for big trains. Three such tunnels run under the ocean between England and France, connecting the two countries beneath the water.

pages.text: The largest vehicle in the world is the Bagger 288. This enormous machine is used for digging in mines and is 705 feet (215 m) long—almost as long as two football fields. Do You Know? People have built enormous vehicles since ancient times. The Helepolis (heh–LEH-puh-lis) was a huge tower built on wheels that was used in battles in ancient Greece. The Helepolis was so heavy that more than three thousand people were needed to move it. Helepolis.
pages.brief: The enormous Bagger 288 digs in a mine, stretching almost as long as two football fields. Nearby, an ancient Greek Helepolis tower on wheels stands ready for battle, so heavy that more than three thousand people are needed to move it.

pages.text: The Bagger digs using a gigantic wheel with buckets along its edge that scoop up dirt as the wheel turns. The Bagger 288 is big enough to move mountains.
pages.brief: The Bagger 288 digs with a gigantic wheel that has buckets along its edge. As the wheel turns, the buckets scoop up dirt. The massive machine works in a mine, looking big enough to move mountains.

pages.text: What will vehicles of the future have to move? This is a design for a bus in China that could drive over other cars. Big Vehicles People use huge vehicles for many different tasks. These amazing vehicles move heavy loads and travel both above and below the ground. Gigantic vehicles have grown in size over the years, and it looks as though they will keep getting bigger and bigger. How big do you think they will get?
pages.brief: A design for a bus in China shows it driving over other cars on a road. Around it, huge vehicles move heavy loads above and below the ground. The gigantic machines have grown bigger over the years and look ready to keep growing.

books.title: Amazing Beaches
books.art_why: The unusual beach features are best shown with clear, stylized drawings.

pages.text: Wow! What a Beach The world has many different types of beaches. Some of them are surprising or amazing.
pages.brief: A wide view of a surprising beach with unusual sand and water, showing that beaches around the world can look very different. The shoreline stretches out beside the ocean, with natural shapes and colors that make the place look amazing.

pages.text: Hot Water Beach Visitors to this beach dig holes in the sand. They’re not making sand castles. They want to sit in the warm water that comes up from beneath the sand.
pages.brief: Visitors on a sandy beach dig holes in the sand around them. They sit in warm water that rises from beneath the sand into the holes, relaxing on the beach instead of building sand castles.

pages.text: Glass Beach Glass items were dumped into the ocean as trash for many years at this beach. The waves and rocks made the glass smooth over time. Today, the glass looks like gems.
pages.brief: Smooth pieces of glass lie scattered on a beach beside rocks and ocean waves. The glass has been worn by waves and rocks over time, so the pieces look like colorful gems resting on the sand.

pages.text: Beach in a Field Not all beaches are found along the shore. This beach is surrounded by land. The water reaches the beach from underground tunnels.
pages.brief: A beach surrounded by land sits in the middle of a field, away from the ocean shore. Water rises onto the sand from underground tunnels beneath the ground, making a beach that is enclosed by open land.

pages.text: Tiny Star Beach The grains of sand at this beach are shaped like tiny stars. They’re really shells that have been worn down into these shapes.
pages.brief: Tiny grains of sand shaped like little stars cover a beach. The star shapes are really small shells that have been worn down over time, lying close together on the sand where they rest.

pages.text: Bowling Ball Beach The round rocks at this beach look like bowling balls. You can visit these amazing rocks during low tide.
pages.brief: Round rocks that look like bowling balls rest on a beach. At low tide the beach is open for people to visit, showing the amazing round rocks sitting together on the sand near the water's edge.

pages.text: Black Sand Beach Rare turtles come to this black sand beach. The sand is black because it’s made of tiny pieces of rock from.
pages.brief: Rare turtles crawl across a beach made of black sand. The black sand is formed from tiny pieces of rock, giving the shore a dark color as the turtles visit this unusual beach beside the ocean.

pages.text: Pink Sand Beach The sand at this beach is the color of cotton candy. The white sand mixes with pieces of red shells to make the sand pink.
pages.brief: Pink sand stretches along a beach, colored like cotton candy. White sand mixes with pieces of red shells to create the pink color, and the soft pink shoreline lies beside the ocean water on the beach.

pages.text: Giant Rock Beach This beach is full of giant rocks. People aren’t the only visitors to this beach. About three thousand penguins live here.
pages.brief: Giant rocks tower over a beach beside the water. People stand together among the huge rocks, and about three thousand penguins also live on this beach, sharing the rocky shore with many human visitors all around.

pages.text: White Sand Beach Have you ever been to a white sand beach? This beach holds the record for being the whitest beach in the world.
pages.brief: A bright white sand beach stretches wide along the ocean under open sky. The sand holds the record as the whitest beach in the world, and the pale shore looks clean and bright beside the calm water.

pages.text: Mile Beach This beach is so long that it’s used as a runway for planes. Be careful when swimming here, though. The water is full of sharks.
pages.brief: A very long beach stretches beside the ocean and is used as a runway for planes. A plane rests on the sand, while sharks swim in the water nearby, making swimming there dangerous for people.

pages.text: Amazing Beaches The sand at beaches can be white, black, red, and even green. Some amazing beaches look as though they’re from other planets. What type of beach would you like to visit?
pages.brief: Several beaches with different sand colors lie side by side: white, black, red, and green. Each shore has its own color, and the sands look strange and wonderful, almost as if these amazing beaches came from other planets far away.

books.title: Whale Sharks: Giant Fish
books.art_why: Real whale sharks, people, and ocean scenes can be photographed.

pages.text: A Very Big Fish The whale shark is the biggest fish in the world. An adult whale shark is as long as a school bus!
pages.brief: An adult whale shark swims through the open ocean, its huge body stretching out as long as a school bus. The giant fish fills the picture, showing that it is the biggest fish in the world.

pages.text: Whale sharks are gentle fish. They are not a danger to people. People safely swim and dive with whale sharks.
pages.brief: Two people in snorkel gear swim and dive safely beside a gentle whale shark in clear ocean water. The whale shark glides calmly past them, showing that whale sharks are not a danger to people.

pages.text: Big Mouth A whale shark has a wide, flat head. It has a huge mouth in the front.
pages.brief: A close view of a whale shark in the ocean shows its wide, flat head and its huge mouth at the front of its face. The giant fish opens its broad mouth as it swims forward.

pages.text: A whale shark’s back is dark with light spots and stripes. Its belly is white. A whale shark has thick skin and sharp scales.
pages.brief: A close-up of a whale shark in the ocean shows its dark back covered with light spots and stripes, its white belly, and thick skin with sharp scales. The fish turns slightly so both sides can be seen.

pages.text: A Warm Bath Whale sharks live in warm oceans around the world. They swim in the middle of the ocean and also close to shore. These giant animals often swim at the surface of the water. They also dive very deep.
pages.brief: A whale shark swims at the sunlit surface of a warm ocean, with the shoreline close by and the middle of the ocean around it. Deep water stretches below, showing that it swims both near shore and far out.

pages.text: Some whale sharks make very long trips. No one knows for sure why. Whale sharks sometimes gather in large groups.
pages.brief: A large group of whale sharks gathers in the open ocean, their long bodies swimming together as they make a very long trip across the water. Some swim close together while others spread out.

pages.text: Mealtime! Whale sharks eat tiny ocean animals and plants. Whale sharks also eat small fish, squid, and fish eggs. Once in a while, they eat bigger fish.
pages.brief: A whale shark feeds in the ocean with its mouth open near clouds of tiny animals and plants, small fish, squid, and fish eggs, while one bigger fish swims nearby. The giant fish moves slowly through the water.

pages.text: Whale sharks do not chew their food. When they open their mouth, their food flows in with the water. Pads near their throat catch the food. Then the water flows out.
pages.brief: A whale shark opens its huge mouth as water and food flow inside. Pads near its throat catch the food, and then the water flows back out without the shark chewing. The food stays in.

pages.text: Giant Babies Whale sharks give birth to live babies. Baby whale sharks are called pups. The pups look like little adult whale sharks.
pages.brief: A mother whale shark swims with her baby whale sharks, called pups, in the ocean. The baby whale sharks are born live, and the pups look like small adult whale sharks as they follow close beside her.

pages.text: Whale sharks grow slowly and live for a long time. They may live to be one hundred years old.
pages.brief: A very large whale shark swims slowly through the ocean, its long body showing that it has grown over many years and may live to be one hundred years old. It moves calmly through the water.

pages.text: Jumbo Fish Whale sharks are special fish. They are huge yet very gentle. Whale sharks are the biggest fish on Earth.
pages.brief: A huge but gentle whale shark swims calmly in the ocean, its giant body filling the scene to show that it is the biggest fish on Earth. This special fish glides slowly past in the blue water.

books.title: Komodo Dragons: Giant Reptiles
books.art_why: Komodo dragons are real animals that exist today and can be photographed.

pages.text: Very Big Lizards Komodo dragons are the biggest lizards in the world. Lizards are reptiles. Snakes, turtles, and alligators are also reptiles.
pages.brief: A very large Komodo dragon stands on dry ground, the biggest lizard in the world. Around it are a snake, a turtle and an alligator, showing other reptiles. The animals are together in one open outdoor scene.

pages.text: Komodo dragons can be as long as two big bathtubs. They are good hunters with sharp teeth and claws.
pages.brief: A Komodo dragon lies stretched out beside two big bathtubs placed end to end, showing its great length. Its sharp teeth and claws are visible as it looks ready to hunt. The scene is outdoors.

pages.text: Ready for a Fight Komodo dragons have long, strong bodies. They use their teeth and claws to get food. They also use their teeth and claws to fight other dragons.
pages.brief: Two Komodo dragons face each other on dry ground, their long, strong bodies braced for a fight. Sharp teeth and claws are visible. One dragon guards a piece of food nearby, showing teeth and claws used to get food.

pages.text: Komodo dragons have hard plates on their bodies. The plates protect them.
pages.brief: A close view of a Komodo dragon shows hard plates covering its body. The dragon stands on dry ground, its armored skin protecting it. The plates look tough and bumpy across its back and sides.

pages.text: What Makes a Komodo Dragon a Reptile? What Makes a Komodo Dragon a Reptile? All reptiles • have a backbone • have scales or bony plates • breathe with lungs Most reptiles • lay eggs • are cold-blooded.
pages.brief: A Komodo dragon stands beside eggs on the ground, showing a reptile with scales and bony plates. Its body is shown in a clear side view. The eggs rest on the ground, and the dragon's mouth is open as it breathes.

pages.text: Hot Home Wild Komodo dragons only live in Asia. They live in forests.
pages.brief: A wild Komodo dragon walks through a forest in Asia. Tall trees and green plants surround it. The dragon's long body moves across the forest floor. This forest is the only kind of home for wild Komodo dragons.

pages.text: The forests can have very hot weather. Komodo dragons stay cool in burrows.
pages.brief: The forest is very hot. A Komodo dragon stays cool inside a burrow in the ground. Its body is partly hidden in the shade of the burrow, while the hot forest is visible outside. The ground around the burrow is dry.

pages.text: Mealtime! Komodo dragons only eat meat. Their favorite foods are deer, wild pigs, and water buffalo. They also eat young dragons!
pages.brief: A Komodo dragon stands near a meal of meat. A deer, a wild pig and a water buffalo are nearby as its favorite foods. A smaller young dragon is also nearby, showing another food it eats.

pages.text: On the Hunt Komodo dragons wait for an animal to pass by. Then they attack with their teeth and claws. The hurt animal runs away and dies. Then the dragons use their tongues to find the dead animal.
pages.brief: A Komodo dragon waits as an animal passes by. It attacks with sharp teeth and claws, and the hurt animal runs away. Later the dragon stands over the dead animal, its tongue out to find it.

pages.text: Baby Dragons Female Komodo dragons lay many eggs in a nest in the ground. They protect the eggs from other animals. The eggs hatch in six to nine months.
pages.brief: A female Komodo dragon lies beside a nest of many eggs in the ground. She guards the eggs from other animals nearby. The eggs rest together in the nest, waiting to hatch in six to nine months.

pages.text: Baby Komodo dragons climb trees to stay safe from adult dragons. They stay there for two years or longer. Male dragons can live to the age of sixty. Female dragons live about half as long.
pages.brief: A baby Komodo dragon climbs a tree, staying safe above adult dragons below. It clings to the trunk and branches. Two adult dragons, one male and one female, stand on the ground nearby. The young dragon stays up there for two years or longer.

pages.text: Jumbo Lizards Komodo dragons are special. They are very strong reptiles. They are the biggest lizards in the world.
pages.brief: A huge Komodo dragon stands on dry ground, showing its strong reptile body. It is the biggest lizard in the world. Its long body and powerful legs make it look special among lizards. The dragon fills the scene.

books.title: Here Come the Cranes!
books.art_why: Sandhill cranes, rivers and farm fields all exist today and are widely photographed.

pages.text: Here Come the Cranes!
pages.brief: A wide view of a flock of tall grey sandhill cranes with red crowns standing together in a shallow wetland, some with wings half open, ready to set off. Soft morning light, green-brown marsh grass and open water behind them.

pages.text: Here Come Cranes! the.
pages.brief: A line of sandhill cranes lifting off the water into the air, long legs trailing and broad wings spread, necks stretched forward. Reeds and open water of a southern marsh below them, pale sky filling most of the picture.

pages.text: Flying North to Nest Sandhill cranes spend the winter in warm areas in the south. They migrate north in the spring. They go north to make nests, lay eggs, and raise chicks.
pages.brief: A sandhill crane standing on a nest of dry grass in a northern marsh, two large eggs and a small chick beside it. Around the nest, flat wet ground, low green plants and open sky, showing the spring nesting place the cranes flew north to reach.

pages.text: Cranes fly north in flocks. They fly many miles each day.
pages.brief: A long flock of sandhill cranes flying in a loose line across a bright sky, wings outstretched, necks reaching forward, all heading the same way. Below them a wide plain of fields and small ponds stretches far into the distance.

pages.text: Eat Up! The cranes get hungry and tired. They need a place to eat and rest. They know just where to go. Wonderful Wings A sandhill crane’s wings reach over 6 feet (1.82 m). A crane can soar on the wind without flapping its wings. It looks as if it’s floating in the sky!
pages.brief: Hungry, tired sandhill cranes landing on a quiet river, some with wings spread wide as they touch down, others standing in the shallow water. In the same scene one crane soars high with wings held still and flat, floating on the wind.

pages.text: The sky grows dark over Nebraska. It’s not a storm. It’s the sandhill cranes!
pages.brief: A huge crowd of sandhill cranes filling the sky above flat Nebraska fields at dusk, thousands of dark wings and long bodies packed from horizon to horizon. The sky is dim with birds, not cloud, and the ground below is open farmland.

pages.text: Sandhill cranes stop at a river. The river offers water, food, and shelter.
pages.brief: Sandhill cranes gathered along a wide shallow river, standing in the water and on the sandy banks. Water spreads across the picture, with plants and muddy edges offering food, and open fields beyond where the birds can rest safely.

pages.text: The cranes eat corn from nearby farm fields. They also eat insects, snails, and frogs.
pages.brief: Sandhill cranes feeding in a harvested farm field, heads down among scattered corn kernels and stubble. Near the water's edge others pick at the ground for insects, snails and frogs, their long beaks reaching into mud and shallow puddles.

pages.text: First Rest, Then Dance At night, the cranes sleep in the river. They stand in the water on their long legs. Predators cannot reach them there.
pages.brief: Night at the river, dark blue water shining under moonlight. Sandhill cranes sleep standing in the shallows on their long legs, bodies still, dozens of them spaced across the water, well away from the banks where predators might walk.

pages.text: The cranes stay at the river for about three weeks. They eat and grow strong. They also dance with each other. Stay Away! A sandhill crane’s long legs make good weapons. The cranes use them to kick attackers that get too close.
pages.brief: Sandhill cranes standing and feeding in a river during the day, one lifting a long leg and kicking it out at a fox-like animal approaching too close. Around them the water, mud and reeds, with other cranes eating and resting nearby.

pages.text: Crane dances are a beautiful sight! The cranes stretch their wings. They bow their heads. They jump high in the air.
pages.brief: Sandhill cranes dancing in an open field: wings stretched wide, heads bowed low, some leaping high off the ground with legs dangling. Several birds dance at once, feathers ruffled, against a clear sky and short green grass.

pages.text: Sandhill cranes dance to find a mate. Most crane mates will stay together for life.
pages.brief: Two sandhill cranes dancing face to face, bowing their heads and spreading their wings toward each other, feet lifted mid-jump. Other cranes stand further back in the field, watching the pair in the open grass under a bright sky.

pages.text: There and Back Again It is time to leave the river. The sandhill cranes fly north. Their calls can be heard for miles. Crane mates build a nest when they reach the north. The mates will raise their chicks together.
pages.brief: Sandhill cranes rising from the river and flying north in a long line, beaks open as they call, wings beating. Far ahead, one pair stands beside a half-built nest of dry grass in a northern marsh with open water around it.

pages.text: The cranes will return to Nebraska in the fall. They will bring their chicks with them. They will stop again to rest and feed. Then they will fly back to the warm waters in the south.
pages.brief: A family group of sandhill cranes standing in a Nebraska river in autumn, two tall adults with a smaller brown chick between them, resting and feeding. Behind them the flat fields stretch out, before the birds fly south again.

books.title: Dragonflies!
books.art_why: Dragonflies and dragonfly parks exist today, so real photographs are possible.

pages.text: Amazing Dragonflies Look! Something small and green is flying fast over the water. It’s a dragonfly!
pages.brief: A small green dragonfly flies fast just above the water, its wings spread wide and its body tilted forward. The water stretches below it, and the dragonfly is the only creature shown, speeding through the open air.

pages.text: What Are Dragonflies? Dragonflies are flying insects with two pairs of wings. They come in many colors. Dragonflies can be green, blue, gold, or even pink.
pages.brief: Several dragonflies hover in open air, each showing two pairs of wings. They appear in different colors: green, blue, gold, and pink. Their thin bodies and four wings are clearly visible as they fly, with each dragonfly separate and easy to compare.

pages.text: Some dragonflies have stripes. Some change color over time.
pages.brief: One dragonfly shows clear stripes across its body and wings. Another dragonfly is shown changing color over time, with one color shifting toward another. Both rest in open air, their wings and patterned bodies easy to see.

pages.text: Dragonflies always live close to water. They lay their eggs in or near water. The young dragonflies live in water for a year or more.
pages.brief: Near the edge of a pond, an adult dragonfly lays eggs in or near the water. Under the water, young dragonflies live in the pond, staying there for a year or more. The pond is their close home.

pages.text: Young Dragonflies Young dragonflies look different from adult dragonflies. They can breathe under the water. Their green and brown colors help them hide from fish, frogs, and other hungry animals.
pages.brief: A young dragonfly looks different from an adult, with a green and brown body. It stays underwater, breathing beneath the surface. Nearby, a fish and a frog swim close, showing the hungry animals it hides from.

pages.text: Super Sight Adult dragonflies have the largest eyes of all the insects. Each eye is made up of about thirty thousand tiny parts. They can see almost all the way around at once.
pages.brief: A close-up of an adult dragonfly's head shows its two enormous eyes. Each eye is made up of thousands of tiny parts across its surface. The dragonfly can see almost all the way around at once.

pages.text: Amazing Flight Dragonflies are some of the fastest flying insects in the world. They can change direction quickly in the air. They can fly forward, backward, and even upside down!
pages.brief: A dragonfly zips through the air, changing direction quickly. It flies forward, then backward, and even upside down, showing why it is one of the fastest flying insects. Its wings blur with speed against the open sky.

pages.text: Amazing Hunters Adult dragonflies hunt small flying insects. They catch these insects from behind and below.
pages.brief: An adult dragonfly hunts a small flying insect. It comes from behind and below, catching the insect in midair. Both are shown in open air, wings spread, with the dragonfly's body stretched toward its tiny prey.

pages.text: They often eat their food in the air. Small insects make good meals!
pages.brief: A dragonfly eats a small insect while flying through the air. The insect is its meal, held near the dragonfly's mouth. The dragonfly's wings stay spread as it feeds in midair, with nothing else around.

pages.text: Dragonflies for Dinner Birds, lizards, frogs, and spiders all like to eat dragonflies. Dragonflies eat other dragonflies, too. Not many animals can catch.
pages.brief: A dragonfly flies near a bird, a lizard, a frog, and a spider, all animals that eat dragonflies. Nearby, one dragonfly catches another dragonfly. The scene shows the many hunters that can catch these insects.

pages.text: Swarms Sometimes dragonflies travel in large groups. These groups are called swarms.
pages.brief: A large swarm of dragonflies travels together through the air. Many dragonflies fill the open space, flying in a group. Their wings and bodies crowd the sky as they move together, many at once, in a swarm.

pages.text: A Safe Place for Dragonflies In 1985, people in Japan created the world’s first dragonfly park. Today there are also dragonfly parks in Europe and the United States. Dragonflies are amazing creatures—and people all over the world are starting to realize it! Dragonflies Worldwide There are nearly three thousand kinds of dragonflies. They are found all around the world. Look at your closest stream, pond, or lake. Maybe you can spot some dragonflies!
pages.brief: People visit a dragonfly park in Japan, walking beside a pond. Dragonflies fly over the water around them. The park is a safe place for dragonflies, and similar parks exist in Europe and the United States.

books.title: Golf
books.art_why: The book mixes old golf history, modern facts and famous players, so drawings suit it.

pages.text: A Quiet Sport Golf is a quiet and fun sport. Players must be calm to play well. They must practice to be good.
pages.brief: A quiet golf setting. A calm player stands on a grassy course, holding a club and practicing a careful swing. The player looks focused and steady, with open green space around, showing that golf is a quiet, fun sport.

pages.text: Playing the Game Players hit a small, hard ball They hit the ball into a small hole in the ground. The player who gets the ball in the hole with the fewest hits wins.
pages.brief: A player hits a small, hard golf ball across the grass toward a small hole in the ground. The ball rolls near the hole. The player watches the shot, ready to count each hit in the game.

pages.text: Players hit the ball hard to try to move it to the green. They may need several hits to get it there.
pages.brief: A golfer hits the ball hard from the grass, trying to send it toward the green. The ball moves across the course. The player may need several more hits before the ball reaches the green.

pages.text: A golf course may have parts with rough grass. The golf course may also have sand or water traps. A player may need more hits to get a ball out of these places.
pages.brief: A golf course shows rough grass, a sandy trap and a water trap. A golfer stands near the rough grass with a club, facing a ball in a difficult spot. The player may need extra hits to get the ball out.

pages.text: Some clubs are good for hitting the ball far away. Others are good for shorter shots.
pages.brief: A set of golf clubs is shown on the grass. One club is held by a golfer ready for a long shot across the course. Other clubs rest nearby on the ground, ready for shorter shots.

pages.text: Each hole of a golf course has a starting place at one end. The green with the small hole is at the other end. A golf course has nine or eighteen holes.
pages.brief: A golf hole is shown from its starting place at one end to the green with the small hole at the other end. A golfer stands at the start, looking down the course. The course has nine or eighteen holes.

pages.text: Golf Long Ago Golf began hundreds of years ago. The first golf balls were made of wood. Now, golf balls are made of rubber and plastic.
pages.brief: Long ago, golfers play with early golf balls made of wood on a grassy course. In a nearby view, modern golf balls made of rubber and plastic rest on the grass, showing how golf balls changed over hundreds of years.

pages.text: Golf Around the World Many people around the world love to play golf. The sport is popular in countries where people speak English.
pages.brief: People around the world play golf on grassy courses. A group of golfers from different places stand together with clubs on the course, ready to play. The sport is shown as popular in countries where people speak English.

pages.text: Golf Contests Some people play in big events. Some events have many contests each year. Men and women play in different golf events.
pages.brief: A big golf event is underway on a course. Men play in one contest, and women play in another, with golfers taking shots toward holes. The scene shows that some events have many contests each year.

pages.text: Famous Golfers Jack Nicklaus is the best golfer ever to play the game. Patty Berg and Tiger Woods are two other great players.
pages.brief: Three great golfers are shown on a course: Jack Nicklaus, Patty Berg and Tiger Woods. Each stands with a club, ready to play. Jack Nicklaus is shown as the best golfer ever, with Patty Berg and Tiger Woods beside him.

pages.text: A Fun Game Funny things can happen in golf. Animals can come very close. Do you want to play? If you practice hard, you can have fun playing golf!
pages.brief: Funny things happen on a golf course. An animal comes very close to a golfer while the player stands with a club on the grass. The golfer smiles, ready to practice hard and have fun playing golf.

books.title: Hockey
books.art_why: Keyword check points to drawing, and the book includes a long-ago hockey history scene.

pages.text: A Fast Sport Hockey is an exciting sport. Hockey players skate very fast on the ice.
pages.brief: Hockey players in team uniforms skate fast across an ice rink, leaning into their strides with sticks in hand. The action shows an exciting sport, with players speeding over the ice together. Their skates carve the ice as they move.

pages.text: Some Game Rules Hockey players play on a team. A hockey team has six players. The team works together to try to win the game.
pages.brief: Six hockey players in matching team uniforms stand together on the ice. They hold their sticks and work as one team, cooperating to try to win the game. The players look toward each other, ready to play together.

pages.text: The game starts in the middle of the ice. A round, black puck is dropped between one player from each team. The two players try to get control of the puck.
pages.brief: At the middle of the ice, two hockey players face each other, one from each team. A round, black puck drops between them, and both players reach with their sticks to control it. Their eyes are on the puck.

pages.text: Players move the puck on the ice with a long stick. They try to hit the puck into a net to score points. The team with more points at the end of the game wins.
pages.brief: Hockey players move a black puck across the ice with long sticks. One player aims the puck toward a net to score points, while teammates follow the play. The team with more points at the end wins.

pages.text: Players try to keep the puck with their team. They try to take the puck from the other team and score a goal. They also try to stop the other team from making a goal.
pages.brief: Two hockey teams compete on the ice. Players try to keep the puck with their own team, take it from the other team, and score a goal. They also try to stop the other team from making a goal.

pages.text: One player on each team stays by the net. This player tries to stop pucks from going into the net. Pucks can move faster than cars on a highway!
pages.brief: One player on each team stays by the net, ready to stop pucks from going in. A puck speeds toward the net faster than a car on a highway, and the player moves to block it.

pages.text: Hockey Long Ago Long ago, people played hockey with a ball. The game was not safe. Players first used a puck in 1875.
pages.brief: Long ago, people play hockey with a ball instead of a puck, and the game looks rough and unsafe. Nearby, an early puck rests in the old scene, showing how hockey changed. The players are from long ago.

pages.text: Hockey Everywhere People in Canada and the United States soon began to play hockey. Now there are thirty top hockey teams in North America.
pages.brief: People in Canada and the United States play hockey. A group of top North American hockey teams is shown, with players in many team uniforms, representing the thirty top teams that now play. The scene shows the sport growing.

pages.text: Seven of these teams are in Canada, and twenty-three are in the United States. Teams play each other to see who is the best.
pages.brief: Seven teams are shown for Canada and twenty-three teams for the United States. Players from two of these teams play each other on the ice, competing to see who is the best. Their uniforms show different team colors.

pages.text: People also play hockey in many other countries. Men, women, girls, and boys can all play hockey.
pages.brief: Men, women, girls, and boys play hockey in many countries. Players of different ages and genders wear hockey gear and hold sticks on the ice, showing that hockey is a sport for everyone. They all enjoy the game.

pages.text: Learning to Play Many communities have teams where you can learn to play hockey. Players first need to learn to skate well. Then they can have fun with this exciting sport!
pages.brief: In a community, players learn to play hockey with a team. They first practice skating well on the ice. Then they play together and have fun with this exciting sport. Their sticks and skates are ready.

books.title: The Measurement Mysteries
books.art_why: Real children, animals and paper clips exist today, so photographs fit.

pages.text: Russell and Joelle have a job to do.
pages.brief: Russell and Joelle stand together as two children with a job to do. They look ready to begin their task, facing forward with a sense of purpose. The scene introduces the two kids and their upcoming job.

pages.text: They need to find out the lengths of different animals. What can they use to measure?
pages.brief: Russell and Joelle think about finding out the lengths of different animals. They look curious and thoughtful, wondering what they can use to measure. The two kids are ready to solve the measuring question together.

pages.text: The kids need items that are the same length. The paper clips will work. The paper clips are equal lengths.
pages.brief: The kids need items that are the same length. Russell and Joelle look at paper clips and see that the paper clips are all equal lengths. The paper clips will work for measuring, so the kids examine the matching clips.

pages.text: How long is Gary the goat?
pages.brief: Russell and Joelle look at Gary the goat. They wonder how long Gary is. The goat stands as the animal the kids want to measure, and the children focus on him. Gary is the animal they will measure first.

pages.text: How many paper clips do the kids need to measure Gary?
pages.brief: Russell and Joelle wonder how many paper clips they need to measure Gary. The kids look at Gary the goat and think about counting paper clips along his length. The two children get ready to find out.

pages.text: They need eight paper clips. Gary is about eight paper clips long.
pages.brief: Russell and Joelle need eight paper clips to measure Gary. Gary the goat is about eight paper clips long. The kids show or count eight paper clips beside Gary as they find his length. They see the result.

pages.text: How long is Wiggles the worm? How many paper clips do the kids need to measure him?
pages.brief: Russell and Joelle look at Wiggles the worm. They wonder how long Wiggles is and how many paper clips they need to measure him. The kids focus on the tiny worm and get ready to measure.

pages.text: They need one paper clip. Wiggles is about one paper clip long. He is shorter than Gary.
pages.brief: Russell and Joelle need one paper clip to measure Wiggles. Wiggles the worm is about one paper clip long. The kids see that Wiggles is shorter than Gary. They compare the worm's length with Gary's.

pages.text: How long is Daisy the dog? How many paper clips do the kids need to measure her?
pages.brief: Russell and Joelle look at Daisy the dog. They wonder how long Daisy is and how many paper clips they need to measure her. The kids focus on the dog and get ready to find her length.

pages.text: They need fourteen paper clips. Daisy is about fourteen paper clips long. She is longer than Gary and Wiggles.
pages.brief: Russell and Joelle need fourteen paper clips to measure Daisy. Daisy the dog is about fourteen paper clips long. The kids see that Daisy is longer than Gary and Wiggles. They count out the paper clips for Daisy.

pages.text: How long is Rosie the rabbit? How many paper clips do the kids need to measure her?
pages.brief: Russell and Joelle look at Rosie the rabbit. They wonder how long Rosie is and how many paper clips they need to measure her. The kids focus on the rabbit and prepare to measure Rosie.

pages.text: They need seven paper clips. Rosie is about seven paper clips long. She is longer than Wiggles. She is shorter than Gary and Daisy.
pages.brief: Russell and Joelle need seven paper clips to measure Rosie. Rosie the rabbit is about seven paper clips long. The kids see that Rosie is longer than Wiggles and shorter than Gary and Daisy. They compare the rabbit's length.

pages.text: The kids measured four animals.
pages.brief: Russell and Joelle have finished measuring four animals. They stand together after their work, with the four animals they measured: Gary the goat, Wiggles the worm, Daisy the dog and Rosie the rabbit. The kids look at the results.

pages.text: What did they find out?
pages.brief: Russell and Joelle think about what they learned from measuring the animals. They look ready to share their findings about the lengths of the four animals. The two kids consider their results together.

pages.text: Which animal is the longest? Which animal is the shortest? What else did Russell and Joelle find out?
pages.brief: Russell and Joelle ask which animal is the longest and which is the shortest. They wonder what else they found out from measuring the four animals. The kids think about their results and look ready to answer the questions.

books.title: Blizzards!
books.art_why: Historical 1888 storm and weather-science scenes suit illustration.

pages.text: The Great White Hurricane In 1888, a blizzard hit New York. The storm lasted for three days. It caused a lot of harm. Many people died.
pages.brief: A wide street in New York City in 1888 during a heavy blizzard. Thick snow covers the road and rooftops. People in long coats and hats lean into the wind, heads down, struggling through deep drifts. Snow blows across the scene, hiding distant buildings.

pages.text: Extreme Storms The United States has had many blizzards. Three things make up a blizzard— strong winds, blinding snow, and freezing cold.
pages.brief: A dramatic winter scene showing the three parts of a blizzard: strong wind bending bare trees, thick blowing snow filling the air, and icy cold frost on a fence. A person bundled in a heavy coat stands hunched against the weather in an open snowy field.

pages.text: Birth of a Blizzard Snow starts when moist warm air meets cold air. Clouds form, and the water in them freezes into snow.
pages.brief: High above a snowy landscape, a mass of moist warm air meets a mass of cold air. Grey clouds form and grow. Inside the clouds, tiny water droplets freeze into ice and snow crystals. Below, bare winter trees and snow-covered ground stretch out.

pages.text: The winds whip the snow through the air. It becomes hard to see.
pages.brief: Snow is whipped through the air by strong winds across an open field. The blowing snow forms a thick white haze. A person in a winter coat walks with arms raised, barely able to see ahead. Trees in the background fade into the swirling white.

pages.text: Biting winds also make air feel colder. This is called wind chill. Wind chill makes the body lose heat faster. Skin can freeze.
pages.brief: A close view of a person outdoors in freezing, windy weather. Sharp wind blows snow around their face and bare hands. Their cheeks and fingers look red and chilled. Frost forms on their scarf. The cold air and wind make the day feel even colder.

pages.text: Blizzard Country Blizzards can happen anywhere there is snow. The East Coast of the United States is one such place.
pages.brief: A wide view of the East Coast of the United States in winter. Snow falls over cities, roads and coastline. Clouds and cold air hang above. Small houses and bare trees stand in snowy fields, showing a cold place where blizzards can happen.

pages.text: Storms sometimes move up from the south. When they do, they may run into cold air moving down from Canada. These storms make lots of snow.
pages.brief: A storm moving up from the south meets cold air pushing down from Canada. Dark clouds collide over a snowy landscape. Snow begins to fall heavily. Below, fields and trees are already white. The meeting of the two air masses brings a thick snowfall.

pages.text: Another type of storm comes from the west. These storms move fast. They bring strong winds and freezing cold, but not a lot of snow.
pages.brief: A fast-moving storm sweeps in from the west across an open plain. Strong winds bend bare trees and drive snow sideways. The sky is dark and cold. A small house stands alone in the snowy field, with snow blowing past its walls. Little snow piles up.

pages.text: Being Prepared and Staying Safe Long ago, people were surprised by storms. Today, people know more about weather. They can tell when and where blizzards will strike.
pages.brief: Weather scientists at work in a forecasting room, studying screens and instruments. One points at a large screen showing swirling storm patterns. Others watch and take notes. Through a window, snowy weather is visible outside. They track where a blizzard will strike.

pages.text: They can get ready. They can make sure they have enough food and water to last for days.
pages.brief: A family at home getting ready for a storm. A parent places cans and boxes of food on a kitchen shelf. A child carries a large bottle of water. More jugs and supplies sit on the counter. Through the window, dark snowy clouds gather over the neighborhood.

pages.text: People can then go home and wait out the storm. There, they can stay safe and warm.
pages.brief: Inside a warm, cozy house during a blizzard. A family sits together in a living room, wrapped in blankets. A fire burns in the fireplace. Outside the window, snow blows hard and the sky is grey. Everyone is safe indoors, waiting for the storm to pass.

pages.text: The best place to be in a blizzard is inside. In time, the storm will end. Then it will be safe to have fun in the snow!
pages.brief: A view from inside a house looking out at a snowy yard after a blizzard. Children in warm coats, hats and boots play in deep snow, making footprints and throwing snowballs. Bare trees and a fence are covered in white. The storm has ended and the sky is clear.

books.title: Acadia National Park
books.art_why: The book includes early Native history and Dorr's story, so drawn scenes fit the historical pages.

pages.text: National P ark ACADIA.
pages.brief: A broad landscape view of Acadia National Park. The park is shown as a whole place, with open space and natural land. No specific animals or people are in focus. The scene gives a simple first look at the park named Acadia.

pages.text: First to See the Sun Maine is the first state to see the Sun rise. In Maine, Acadia National Park is one of the places to see it first.
pages.brief: The Sun rises over Maine and Acadia National Park. The first light of morning spreads across the park. The land is quiet as the new day begins. Acadia is shown as one of the places in Maine where the sunrise can be seen first.

pages.text: Land That Meets the Sea Millions of people visit Acadia each year. They come to see the Sun rise on its tall peaks. They come to see its islands and forests. They come to see its lakes and rocky coast.
pages.brief: Many visitors spread across Acadia National Park. Some stand on tall peaks watching the sunrise. Others look out toward islands, forests, lakes, and the rocky coast where land meets the sea. The park is busy with people taking in these different views.

pages.text: Tide pools form on Acadia’s beaches when the tide goes out. The tide pools are home to many living things.
pages.brief: Tide pools form on a beach in Acadia after the tide goes out. Shallow pools of water sit among the rocks and sand. Small living things are visible in the pools. The beach is quiet, and the tide pools are shown as homes for these creatures.

pages.text: Wildlife Acadia is a great place to watch birds. Some fly over as they head south. Other birds live in the park all year. People have seen hundreds of kinds of birds there.
pages.brief: People watch birds in Acadia National Park. Some birds fly overhead as they head south. Other birds stay in the park all year. The watchers look toward the birds, and many different kinds of birds are shown around the park.

pages.text: Return of the Falcon Peregrine falcons are one of the fastest animals on Earth. Human actions killed many of the birds. Acadia worked hard to bring them back. Now falcon chicks are born in the park every year.
pages.brief: A peregrine falcon, one of the fastest animals on Earth, is shown in Acadia National Park. Falcon chicks are born in the park. The adult falcon and chicks are together in a natural setting. The scene shows the birds back in the park after people worked to bring them back.

pages.text: Acadia is home to many mammals, too. Some of those mammals live in the water and on land.
pages.brief: A mammal is shown at the edge of the water in Acadia, with its body near both the water and the land. It is in a place where water and land meet. The scene shows that some mammals in the park live in both places.

pages.text: Some of those mammals live in the forest.
pages.brief: A mammal is shown in the forest of Acadia National Park. It moves among the trees and undergrowth. The forest is its home. The scene shows that some of the park's mammals live in the forest.

pages.text: Some of those mammals live in the ground.
pages.brief: A mammal is shown in Acadia National Park near the ground. It stays close to the soil, where it lives. The scene shows that some of the park's mammals make their home in the ground. The setting is natural and quiet.

pages.text: A Park Made Piece by Piece Native people protected this land for years. Then Maine became a state. Rich people bought land along its coast. Soon, many different people owned bits of the area.
pages.brief: Native people are shown protecting the land that would become Acadia. Later, Maine becomes a state. Rich people buy land along the coast. Soon many different people own bits of the area. The scene shows the land being divided among many owners.

pages.text: Some of those people wanted to protect the area. They donated the land to the government. In 1919, that land became a national park. The Story of Dorr George Dorr lived alone on Mount Desert Island. Over time, he bought lots of land. Then he donated it. He had spent all his money by the time he died in 1944. But Dorr had made his dream come true. Acadia had become a national park. In fact, it is still growing today, piece by piece.
pages.brief: George Dorr is shown alone on Mount Desert Island. He buys lots of land over time and then gives it away. Other people also give land to the government. In 1919 the land becomes a national park. Dorr is shown having spent his money to make his dream come true. The park is shown still growing piece by piece today.

pages.text: Conclusion There is plenty to see and do in Acadia. Some people come to see the Sun rise. Some people come to see the land meet the sea. Some people come to hike, climb, fish, or ride a bicycle.
pages.brief: Visitors enjoy Acadia National Park in different ways. Some come to see the sunrise. Some come to see the land meet the sea. Others hike, climb, fish, or ride a bicycle. The park is shown full of things to see and do.

pages.text: If you ever get the chance to visit, do!
pages.brief: A welcoming view of Acadia National Park invites a visit. The park is shown as a place worth seeing, with open land and natural scenery. No specific activity is in focus. The scene simply suggests that a person should visit if the chance comes.

books.title: Rocky Mountain National Park
books.art_why: The book shows a real national park that exists today, with photographable mountains, lakes, forests, and wildlife.

pages.text: Rocky Mountain National Park.
pages.brief: A wide landscape view of a national park with tall mountains in the background, a calm lake in the middle, and green forests spreading across the land. The sky is clear and bright. No people or animals are shown; the scene focuses on the park's natural scenery.
