pages.text: The Best of the Rockies Rocky Mountain National Park has many high mountains. It has lakes and forests. The air is fresh and clean. The park is home to many wild animals.
pages.brief: A wide view of Rocky Mountain National Park shows several high mountain peaks, a lake, and green forests. The air looks fresh and clean. In the foreground, a few wild animals stand among the trees, and birds fly in the clear sky.

pages.text: Young Mountains The national park is a small part of the Rocky Mountains. The Rocky Mountains are a big mountain range. It formed millions of years ago. It is still young for a mountain range!
pages.brief: A vast mountain range with many peaks stretches across the landscape. In the foreground, a smaller area of mountains and valleys suggests the national park within the larger range. The scene is wide and open, showing the great scale of the Rocky Mountains.

pages.text: The tops of the park’s tallest mountains do not have trees. It is too cold for trees to grow that high. Many flowers grow there in summer, though.
pages.brief: The high tops of the park's tallest mountains are bare, with no trees growing. The ground is rocky and cold. In summer, colorful flowers bloom across the high alpine ground, adding patches of color to the rocky landscape. The sky is clear above the peaks.

pages.text: From Moose to Marmots Many kinds of birds live in the park. Some birds fly on mountain winds. Some birds stay on the ground. In summer, one bird turns brown. In winter, it turns white as snow.
pages.brief: Several birds are shown in the park. Some birds soar on mountain winds high above the peaks. Other birds stay on the ground among rocks and low plants. One bird is shown in brown summer feathers, and the same bird is shown in white winter feathers, blending with snow.

pages.text: Different mammals live in different parts of the park. Some mammals live in its fields and forests.
pages.brief: Mammals are shown in the park's fields and forests. A deer stands in a grassy field, and a small mammal is near the trees. The animals are in their natural habitats, with green plants and trees around them. The scene shows different mammals in different parts of the park.

pages.text: Some mammals live above where trees can grow.
pages.brief: High above the tree line, where trees no longer grow, a mammal is shown on rocky ground. The landscape is open and rocky, with low plants and scattered stones. The animal stands or moves among the rocks in the cold, high environment.

pages.text: Plan a Visit This road goes from one side of the park to the other. The road climbs very high.
pages.brief: A road curves and climbs through the mountain landscape, going from one side of the park toward the other. The road is empty, surrounded by steep slopes and forests. The high mountains rise above the road.

pages.text: Some people like to get away from cars. Some put their tents near lakes. Some climb the park’s tallest mountain.
pages.brief: People are enjoying the park away from cars. Some people set up tents near a lake. Others climb the park's tallest mountain, walking up a rocky trail. The scene shows both camping and hiking in the natural landscape.

pages.text: Autumn is a special time to visit the park. Leaves turn bright yellow. People also come to see and hear elk.
pages.brief: In autumn, the park's leaves turn bright yellow. People stand in a group, watching and listening to elk nearby. The elk are visible among the yellow trees. The scene shows the special autumn colors and the visitors observing the animals.

pages.text: History of Rocky Mountain National Park Native peoples once lived in and traveled through the land that is now Rocky Mountain National Park. They camped in the beautiful valleys during the summer. Other people started to move there in the mid-1800s. Some were looking for gold. For people moving west in wagons, these steep mountains were hard to cross. In 1915, the president signed a law creating this national park.
pages.brief: Native peoples are shown camping in a green valley in summer. In another scene, people in covered wagons move west across steep mountain trails, some looking for gold. A president signs a document in 1915, creating the national park.

pages.text: A Popular Park Millions of people visit the park each year. During the summer, some parts of the park get crowded.
pages.brief: Many visitors fill a part of the park during summer. People walk along a trail and gather near a viewpoint. The area looks crowded with families and tourists. The mountains and trees are in the background.

pages.text: Still, in this park, there are always ways to escape into nature.
pages.brief: A quiet, empty corner of the park shows a path leading into nature. No people are visible. Trees, rocks, and mountains create a peaceful scene where someone could escape the crowds and enjoy the wild landscape.

books.title: Dolphins
books.art_why: Dolphins are real animals that exist today.

pages.text: Introduction Dolphins live in every ocean in the world. Some even live in rivers.
pages.brief: Several dolphins swim in open ocean water, with one dolphin shown in a river setting nearby, illustrating that dolphins live in every ocean and some in rivers. The scene shows only dolphins and water, with no other animals or people.

pages.text: Dolphins Are Mammals Dolphins are mammals. They can keep their body warm. Dolphin mothers make milk for babies. They do not lay eggs. Instead, their babies are born live.
pages.brief: A dolphin mother swims beside her live-born baby in the ocean. The baby stays close to her body, showing a dolphin mammal family. No egg is shown; the scene focuses on the mother and baby in the water.

pages.text: Dolphins breathe in air through a hole on their head. Most of the time, dolphins breathe They can hold their breath for more than a minute when they need to. Wowser! Dolphins don’t sleep for hours at a time like most animals. Instead, they rest part of their brain for fifteen to twenty minutes at a time. Because parts of their brain are still working, dolphins stay near the surface while asleep. This way, they can get air when they need it. While they sleep, dolphins even keep one eye open!
pages.brief: A dolphin floats near the ocean surface with its blowhole above the water, taking in air. Its body is relaxed as it rests part of its brain, and one eye remains open. The water surface and the dolphin’s head are the main focus.

pages.text: All About Dolphins Dolphins are different sizes. They can be big or small. Do You Know? There are almost forty kinds of dolphins. Killer whales, or orcas, are the largest. They can be 10 meters (32 ft.) long. Maui (MOW-ee) are the smallest type of dolphin. They are only 1 meter (4 ft.) long.
pages.brief: Dolphins of different sizes swim together in the ocean. A large killer whale, or orca, appears beside a tiny Maui dolphin, showing the biggest and smallest kinds. The water around them is clear, with the size difference easy to see.

pages.text: Some dolphins only have four teeth. Others have more than two hundred teeth! Dolphins do not use their teeth to chew. They use their teeth to grab food. Then they eat it whole.
pages.brief: Two dolphins swim in the ocean, one with a small number of visible teeth and one with many teeth. One dolphin grabs food with its teeth and swallows it whole rather than chewing. The scene focuses on the dolphin’s mouth and the food it takes.

pages.text: Dolphins move their tail up and down to swim. A fin on their back keeps them steady. A flipper on each side helps them steer.
pages.brief: A dolphin swims through the ocean, its tail moving up and down. A fin on its back stays steady while a flipper on each side helps it steer. The dolphin’s body is shown clearly in the water as it moves forward.

pages.text: Dolphins and Sound Dolphins are smart. Dolphins use sound to talk to other dolphins. Dolphins also use sound to find food.
pages.brief: Two dolphins face each other in the ocean, using sound to communicate. Nearby, a dolphin sends sound toward food, showing how sound helps it find a meal. The scene focuses on dolphins, water and sound waves in the sea.

pages.text: Dolphin Groups Dolphins live in groups called pods. They live in pods to find food and keep each other safe.
pages.brief: A pod of dolphins swims together in the ocean. Several dolphins stay close as they search for food, and their grouping helps keep each other safe. The water surrounds the pod, with all dolphins moving in the same direction.

pages.text: Dolphins move from pod to pod. Sometimes they change pods more than once a day.
pages.brief: Dolphins swim in the ocean as one pod separates and another pod approaches. A dolphin moves from one group to another, showing that dolphins change pods sometimes more than once a day. The scene shows several dolphin groups in the water.

pages.text: Mothers form pods with other mothers to protect their babies. Even after they leave, young dolphins may return to swim with their mother. Some female dolphins even return to raise their babies with their own mother.
pages.brief: Several dolphin mothers swim together with their babies in a protected pod. One mother stays close to her young, and a grown young dolphin swims near its mother again. The group shows mothers and babies staying together in the ocean.

pages.text: Conclusion There are many different kinds of dolphins. They all use sound to talk and find food. Most dolphins form close groups. Dolphins are amazing animals!
pages.brief: Many kinds of dolphins swim in the ocean, using sound to talk and find food. Several dolphins form close groups, or pods, as they move through the water. The scene brings together different dolphins and their family groups.

books.title: Istanbul
books.art_why: Historical city landmarks and past events are shown through drawn scenes.

pages.text: One City, Two Worlds A ship sails into a big city. Parts of the city are in Europe. Other parts are in Asia. This is Istanbul, Turkey. Wowser! Istanbul is on two continents. Continents are Earth’s huge pieces of land. Only a few other cities are on two continents.
pages.brief: A ship sails into a big city on the water. On one side of the city, people and buildings sit in Europe; on the other side, they sit in Asia. The city is Istanbul, Turkey, and it spreads across two continents, shown as two huge pieces of land.

pages.text: Where in the World? Istanbul is on the water. It has the most people of any city in Europe.
pages.brief: Istanbul sits beside the water, with buildings and streets close to the shore. Many people fill the city, more than in any other city in Europe. Boats move on the water, and the busy city spreads out along the edge.

pages.text: Istanbul is an important city. It brings together people from different places.
pages.brief: People from many different places come together in Istanbul. They walk through busy streets and share the same city spaces. The city is important because it brings people from different places together in one lively place.

pages.text: History Istanbul has had other names. It became Istanbul in 1930. Let’s visit some parts of this city. Istanbul’s Other Names Long ago, Istanbul was called Byzantium (bih-ZAN-tee-uhm). It was named for a leader named Byzas. Later, it was called Constantinople. It was named for a ruler named Constantine the Great.
pages.brief: An old city view shows Istanbul as it looked long ago. A leader named Byzas stands near the early city called Byzantium. Later, the city is called Constantinople for the ruler Constantine the Great. In 1930, the city becomes Istanbul, and visitors begin to explore its parts.

pages.text: A Space for Water This huge space is under the ground. Long ago, it was filled with water. People used the water for many things.
pages.brief: A huge underground space lies beneath the city. Long ago, water filled this large room. People used the water for many things. The space is shown deep under the ground, with water inside and the city above it.

pages.text: Market This huge market is made of stone. The first parts were built in 1461. Other parts were built later. The market has many shops. Wowser! • The market has 61 covered streets. • It has more than 4,000 shops. • More than 250,000 people shop here every day.
pages.brief: A huge stone market fills a busy city area. Its first parts were built in 1461, and more parts were added later. Many shops line the covered streets. Crowds of people shop here every day, moving past shop after shop in the big market.

pages.text: Island Tower This old tower is on a small island. First, people used it to watch ships. Later, its lights helped ships. Today, people eat here.
pages.brief: An old tower stands on a small island in the water. Long ago, people used the tower to watch ships. Later, its lights helped ships find their way. Today, people sit and eat at the island tower, with water all around.

pages.text: Tall Tower This tall tower was built in 1348. People have used it in many ways. Today, people climb the stairs inside to look at the city.
pages.brief: A tall tower rises above Istanbul. It was built in 1348 and people have used it in many ways. Today, people climb the stairs inside the tower. From the top, they look out over the city and its buildings.

pages.text: Huge Palace This palace is very old. Many rulers lived here. Now it is a museum. High walls are around the outside.
pages.brief: A huge old palace stands behind high walls. Many rulers lived here long ago. Today, the palace is a museum. People visit and walk around the outside, where the high walls surround the old royal home.

pages.text: Grand Museum This huge building was first built It later became a mosque and then Today, it is a mosque again.
pages.brief: A very large old building stands in the city. It was first built long ago. Later, it became a mosque. Today, it is a mosque again. The huge building is shown as an important place in the city.

pages.text: City Square This city square was built in the 1700s. Today, it has shops and places to eat.
pages.brief: A city square is shown with open space in the middle. It was built in the 1700s. Today, shops and places to eat stand around the square. People move through the square, stopping at shops and eating places in the busy city center.

pages.text: A Trip Back in Time Istanbul has many great places to see. Each place has a story to tell. Going there is like taking a trip back in time.
pages.brief: Istanbul has many great places to see. Each place has a story to tell. A visitor looks out over the city and its old places, as if taking a trip back in time. The city spreads out with many places waiting to be explored.

books.title: The Everglades
books.art_why: Real animals, plants, people, and places that exist today.

pages.text: Weird and Wonderful The Everglades is in South Florida. It has hot, wet summers. It has mild, dry winters. Water, plants, and animals are everywhere.
pages.brief: A wide view of the Everglades in South Florida under a hot, bright summer sun. Shallow water spreads between green plants, and animals are visible among the reeds and trees. The air feels wet and warm, with water, plants, and wildlife filling the scene.

pages.text: More Than a Swamp The Everglades has many different areas. Some areas have fresh water. Tall trees grow there.
pages.brief: A freshwater area of the Everglades. Tall trees grow beside calm water, their trunks rising from the wetland. Green plants crowd the water’s edge. The scene shows a fresh, wet habitat where trees and water sit together under a soft sky.

pages.text: Some areas have salt water. The trees that grow there have long roots.
pages.brief: A saltwater area of the Everglades. Trees with long, tangled roots stand in the water, holding onto the muddy shore. The roots arch and dip into the salt water. Small waves ripple past the roots while the trees rise above the surface.

pages.text: Some areas have tall plants called Their leaves are sharp, like Some areas have woods. Tall trees there grow close together.
pages.brief: Tall plants with sharp, blade-like leaves grow thickly in one area of the Everglades. Nearby, a wooded patch holds tall trees growing close together. The sharp-leaved plants stand in water, while the woods form a dense wall of trunks and leaves.

pages.text: A Park Is Born For a long time, the Everglades did not change. Then, some people wanted to farm the land. They also wanted to build homes there. River of Grass In the 1940s, a woman named Marjory Stoneman Douglas wrote a book called The Everglades: River of Grass. The book was a big success. It helped save the special nature of the area.
pages.brief: A woman named Marjory Stoneman Douglas writes her book, The Everglades: River of Grass, in the 1940s. In the same view, people farm the land and build homes in the Everglades. The scene shows the writer and the changing land together.

pages.text: Other people thought this was bad. They worked hard to save the Everglades. In 1947, part of the Everglades.
pages.brief: People who thought the changes were bad work hard to save the Everglades. They stand together in the wetland, focused on protecting the land and water. In the background, part of the Everglades stretches out in 1947, with plants and water around them.

pages.text: Protecting the Park Making the park was just the beginning. The Everglades still needs help. Changing weather is a problem. It is hard on the plants and animals that live there.
pages.brief: Dark clouds gather over Everglades National Park as changing weather brings strong wind and heavy rain. Plants bend, and animals seek shelter among the reeds and trees. The wet, wild scene shows how hard the changing weather can be on the park’s plants and animals.

pages.text: Some plants and animals were brought to the Everglades from other places. They make it harder for Everglades plants and animals to live.
pages.brief: Thick, unfamiliar plants crowd a wetland in the Everglades, brought from other places. They grow over and around native plants, making space tight. Native animals stand among the dense growth, finding it harder to move and live as the new plants spread.

pages.text: Into the Wild People come from all over to visit the Everglades. They walk on the trails. They ride boats on the water. A park visitor kayaks through the swamps.
pages.brief: Visitors explore the Everglades in different ways. Some walk along a trail beside the water, some ride in a boat on the water, and one visitor kayaks through the swamp. Plants and water surround them as they move through the park.

pages.text: They see the amazing sights. Beautiful birds, animals, and plants are everywhere.
pages.brief: Visitors stop to look at the amazing sights around them. Beautiful birds perch and fly near the water, animals move among the plants, and green plants fill the wetland. The visitors take in the bright, lively scene spread out before them.

pages.text: Those things are what make Everglades National Park special. It is a park like no other.
pages.brief: A wide view of Everglades National Park shows the special sights that make it a park like no other. Water, plants, birds, and animals spread across the landscape. The open wetland and its wildlife fill the scene, showing why the park stands apart.

pages.text: Everglades National Park by the Numbers  1.5 million acres (607,000 ha)  Over 1 million visitors each year  Over 360 types of birds  About 120 types of trees  More than 40 types of mammals  More than 50 kinds of reptiles.
pages.brief: A broad view of Everglades National Park shows many birds in the sky and trees across the land. Different mammals and reptiles appear near the water and among the plants. The scene reflects the park’s huge size and the great variety of wildlife living there.

books.title: Badlands National Park
books.art_why: Badlands National Park exists today and can be photographed.

pages.text: Badlands National Park.
pages.brief: A broad view of Badlands National Park, with rugged, eroded landforms stretching across the scene under an open sky. The landscape looks dry and rocky, with no people in view, giving a sense of the park as a wide natural place.

pages.text: Badlands National Park South Dakota Badlands National Park Ben Reifel Visitor Center Badlands National Park White River Visitor Center On a map, Badlands National Park has an odd, skinny shape. That’s because it’s made up of three parts.
pages.brief: An overhead map view shows South Dakota with the odd, skinny outline of Badlands National Park split into three connected parts. Two visitor-center buildings appear at their places in the park: Ben Reifel Visitor Center and White River Visitor Center. Open land surrounds the park shape.

pages.text: Water and wind created the Badlands. Those forces are still hard at work there today. What’s Good About the Badlands? Badlands National Park is a strange and beautiful place.
pages.brief: Wind blows across a rocky Badlands slope while water runs through a channel, shaping the strange, beautiful land. The scene shows the forces still at work on the rocks and dry ground, with open sky above and no people present.

pages.text: The Park The park is in South Dakota. Many people visit it each year. The park is called Badlands because the land is rocky and dry. It is a special place. Land of the Lakota The Lakota are a Native American group. They live in parts of the park. They call the area mako sica (mah-KOH SHEE-chah). It means “land that is bad.”
pages.brief: A rocky, dry landscape in South Dakota has a few visitors looking out over the park. Nearby, a Lakota person stands on the land, representing the Native American group that lives in parts of the park and calls the area mako sica.

pages.text: Rocks and Grass Scientists study the land in the park. Layers of rock show the scientists how it formed. The layers of rock are different colors. Each layer tells a story about the past.
pages.brief: Scientists stand beside a cliff of layered rock in the park, studying the different colored bands. Grass grows nearby. The rock layers rise in clear steps, and the scientists look closely at how the land formed, with open sky above.

pages.text: Fossils can be found in the layers. Fossils were once plants and animals. They have turned to rock. Fossils show that the park used to be a jungle. Before that, the park was underwater.
pages.brief: Fossils of ancient plants and animals are embedded in bands of layered rock. The stone holds clear fossil shapes, and the layers are exposed in a cliff. The scene suggests the park was once a jungle and, before that, underwater.

pages.text: Part of the park is grassy. Very few trees grow there. The grassy part is called a prairie.
pages.brief: A broad prairie of grass stretches across part of the park, with very few trees in sight. The grassy land rolls gently under a wide sky, and the open space shows the prairie that makes up this part of Badlands National Park.

pages.text: Beasts of the Badlands Many animals make their homes in the park. Sheep climb the cliffs. Rattlesnakes move around the rocks.
pages.brief: Sheep climb up a rocky cliff in the park, their hooves gripping the stone. Below, a rattlesnake moves around rocks on the ground. The animals are in their park homes among cliffs and loose rock under an open sky.

pages.text: Most wild animals live in the grassy part of the park. Wild animals find food there.
pages.brief: Wild animals move through the grassy part of the park, finding food among the plants. The prairie stretches around them, with no trees in view, and the animals stay in the open grassland where most of the park’s wildlife lives.

pages.text: Prairie dogs pop out of holes. They warn of danger.
pages.brief: Prairie dogs pop out of holes in the ground, standing alert on the grassy prairie. One prairie dog looks around while others stay near their burrows, ready to warn of danger. The small animals are surrounded by open grass and soft earth.

pages.text: Many birds live in the park, too. The animals are safe in the park. No one can hunt them there.
pages.brief: Several birds fly and perch in the park, sharing the land with other animals. The animals rest and move without threat, safe in the park where no one can hunt them. Open sky and grassy ground surround the birds and wildlife.

pages.text: Planning a Visit Badlands National Park is a great road trip. Many visitors see it from their cars. A long road runs through the park.
pages.brief: A long road runs through Badlands National Park. Visitors see the park from their cars as they drive along the road, with rocky land and open sky around them. The scene shows a road trip through the park, with cars moving through the wide landscape.

pages.text: There are many places to stop and take pictures. The Badlands are bad and beautiful.
pages.brief: Visitors stop at a viewpoint in Badlands National Park and take pictures of the rocky, beautiful land. A few people stand together, holding cameras and looking out over the strange landscape. The open view shows why the Badlands are called bad and beautiful.

books.title: Tian Tian, a Giant Panda
books.art_why: Tian Tian is a real living giant panda at a zoo today, so photographs exist.

pages.text: Tian Tian, a Giant Panda.
pages.brief: One giant panda stands alone in a soft, open space, facing the viewer. His fur is black and white, thick and shaggy, and his round face is calm. His dark paws rest on the ground and his heavy head is lifted a little.

pages.text: This is Tian Tian. He is a giant panda. Most giant pandas have black and white fur like Tian Tian.
pages.brief: Tian Tian, a giant panda, sits on the ground with his black and white fur clearly visible: black ears, black legs, black shoulders and a pale round belly. He looks straight at the viewer with one front paw lifted, in a simple grassy enclosure.

pages.text: Tian Tian has black fur around his eyes. Raccoons have black fur around their eyes, too. But Tian Tian is not a raccoon. All giant pandas are bears.
pages.brief: Close view of Tian Tian's face, showing the black fur ringing his round eyes. Beside him a raccoon also has dark fur around its eyes as it stands on a log. Both animals face forward, the panda's heavy bear body filling the other side.

pages.text: Tian Tian was born in China. He now lives at a zoo in the United States. He came to the United States when he was three years old. In China, he lived at a special place for pandas.
pages.brief: Tian Tian the giant panda stands in his zoo enclosure in the United States, on grass with rocks and a climbing frame behind him. He is large and calm, shown in a wide view of the fenced home where he now lives.

pages.text: China is the only place where wild giant pandas live. They live in mountain forests. There are only about 1,600 wild giant pandas in China.
pages.brief: Wild giant pandas sit among tall trees and thick bamboo on a green mountain slope in China. Two or three pandas rest and chew, spaced apart from one another, with mist over the forested mountains behind them and no people in sight.

pages.text: All giant pandas eat a plant called bamboo. Bamboo grows in the mountain forests in China. More people are cutting down the forests. Without bamboo, giant pandas cannot survive.
pages.brief: Green bamboo stalks grow tall and leafy in a Chinese mountain forest, and a giant panda reaches for a stalk. Behind it a cleared patch shows bare stumps and open ground where trees have been cut down beside the remaining forest.

pages.text: Tian Tian eats bamboo. He can eat 40 pounds of bamboo every day. He also eats biscuits. He eats special fruit popsicles, too.
pages.brief: Tian Tian sits back on the grass holding a thick bamboo stalk and stripping the leaves with his teeth, a pile of chewed stalks beside him. On the ground nearby lie a few round biscuits and a coloured fruit popsicle.

pages.text: Weight Chart Tian Tian is very big and strong. He weighs 275 pounds. That’s as much as 34 cats.
pages.brief: Tian Tian stands squarely, big and strong, his heavy body and thick legs filling the frame. Around him on the grass sit many cats, arranged one row after another, showing how much he weighs compared with them.

pages.text: Tian Tian turned eight years old in 2005. He became a father in 2005, too. His baby was born at the zoo. The baby is growing strong like Tian Tian.
pages.brief: Tian Tian lies on the ground at the zoo beside a small panda cub. The cub is young and fuzzy, pressing close against the adult's side, while Tian Tian's big head rests near it. Grass and rocks of the enclosure surround them.

pages.text: Tian Tian stays strong by playing. He plays with toys. He also plays in trees. Do you like to play? How is Tian Tian like you?
pages.brief: Tian Tian plays in a zoo yard, pushing a large ball and a sturdy toy along the ground. Nearby he has climbed partway up a tree trunk, gripping it with strong claws, branches above him and grass and rocks below.
